title: Why Students Cheat with AI
author: Paul Matthews
summary: This piece reframes AI-driven cheating as a task-design problem rather than purely a discipline or character problem, opening with a deliberately inverted thought experiment: what specific design choices would maximize the 'outsourceability' of an assessment -- arbitrary framing, ambiguous instructions with no worked examples, a task pitched either far out of reach or trivially boring, and long, unmonitored windows between assignment and due date. From that inverted diagnostic, the author derives four positive factors that reduce outsourcing: 'formational clarity' (being explicit that a task's purpose is to shape the kind of person a student becomes, not just to produce a deliverable), 'task clarity' (concrete examples and non-examples of what a good response looks like, since ambiguity is what makes outsourcing tempting in the first place), 'capability' (calibrating task difficulty to a student's genuine reach, illustrated by a marathon-versus-mile analogy paralleling the Zone of Proximal Development), and 'visibility' (breaking a task into monitored checkpoints so the academic process, not just the final product, stays observable to the teacher). The piece closes with a candid acknowledgment that no amount of good task design eliminates misconduct entirely, framing the goal instead as a probabilistic 'numbers game': shifting the large middle band of students who would outsource a poorly-designed task but genuinely engage with a well-designed one, while accepting that some students will cheat regardless and others never would have anyway.
points: The inverted thought experiment -- deliberately designing a maximally 'outsourceable' task (arbitrary, ambiguous, either too hard or too easy, and unmonitored for two weeks) -- functions as a diagnostic checklist teachers can run their own existing assignments against, rather than a vague warning to 'watch for cheating.'

'Formational clarity' reframes the purpose of an assignment away from 'produce this work' toward 'become this kind of person,' arguing that when students only see the former, outsourcing production to AI feels costless since the deeper purpose was never made visible to them.

The marathon-versus-mile analogy operationalizes capability calibration: a student won't outsource a task within their genuine reach (the mile) the way they would one pitched beyond it (the marathon), directly linking task difficulty design to the likelihood of AI misuse.

The closing 'numbers game' framing sets a realistic, falsifiable goal for task redesign: not eliminating misconduct (which good design cannot do, any more than good housing design eliminates vandalism), but shifting the large middle band of students who would outsource a poor task yet engage with a well-designed one.
quotes: Outsourceability is the quality in an assessment that makes it easy for a student to produce the required work without doing the required thinking.
Students default to thinking that the purpose of school is to produce work. But the purpose of school is to produce people. Every task we give is actually doing something to our learners.
If students have a clear example of 'What A Good One Looks Like', they're less likely to pull the intellectual parachute and outsource it to AI.
Now - if you have a robot that can run the marathon in your place - would you outsource the run? Of course. But what if you had to run a mile instead? You might actually do it.
When it comes to AI misuse, daylight is the best disinfectant. Transparent process encourages honest work.

I know there is a student out there who would outsource a poorly designed task yet engage with a well designed task, and that's the sort of student we're after. Some students will try to outsource no matter what.
